title: Schneeweißchen und Rosenroth
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 161. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (daß, gieng, roth, Rath).
about: KHM 161 follows two devoted sisters — gentle Schneeweißchen and lively Rosenroth — who live alone with their widowed mother and befriend a bear that visits their cottage each winter. Through the warmer months the girls repeatedly rescue a bad-tempered dwarf from small mishaps of his own making and are cursed at for their trouble every time, until the bear finally settles accounts with him and turns out to be an enchanted prince. This is not the Snow White of KHM 53 (Schneewittchen) — the English names look alike but the two heroines and stories are unrelated.

sentences.t: Eine arme Wittwe, die lebte einsam in einem Hüttchen, und vor dem Hüttchen war ein Garten, darin standen zwei Rosenbäumchen, davon trug das eine weiße, das andere rothe Rosen:
sentences.l: A poor widow, she lived alone in a little cottage, and before the cottage was a garden, therein stood two little rose-trees, of which the one bore white, the other red roses:
sentences.i: A poor widow lived alone in a little cottage, and before the cottage was a garden, in which stood two little rose-trees, one bearing white roses, the other red:
sentences.n: “Wittwe” and “rothe” keep the 1857 spellings of Witwe and rote. “die lebte” picks the widow up with a resumptive ‘she’ — common in older narrative, dropped in smooth English.

sentences.t: und sie hatte zwei Kinder, die glichen den beiden Rosenbäumchen, und das eine hieß Schneeweißchen, das andere Rosenroth.
sentences.l: and she had two children, who resembled the two little rose-trees, and the one was called Snow-white, the other Rose-red.
sentences.n: The names are kept untranslated in the text; their sense is in the glossary. “glichen” is from “gleichen” (to resemble) + dative, ‘resembled the rose-trees.’

sentences.t: Sie waren aber so fromm und gut, so arbeitsam und unverdrossen, als je zwei Kinder auf der Welt gewesen sind:
sentences.l: But they were as devout and good, as industrious and untiring, as ever two children in the world have been:
sentences.n: “fromm” here is the older sense ‘good, well-behaved, dutiful,’ not narrowly ‘pious.’ “als je” = as ever.

sentences.t: Schneeweißchen war nur stiller und sanfter als Rosenroth.
sentences.l: Snow-white was only quieter and gentler than Rose-red.
sentences.n: Comparatives “stiller … sanfter als.” “nur” = only, marking the single difference between them.

sentences.t: Rosenroth sprang lieber in den Wiesen und Feldern umher, suchte Blumen und fieng Sommervögel:
sentences.l: Rose-red preferred to spring about in the meadows and fields, sought flowers and caught butterflies:
sentences.i: Rose-red liked better to romp about the meadows and fields, hunting flowers and catching butterflies:
sentences.n: “lieber” (rather, by preference) is the comparative of ‘gern.’ “Sommervögel” literally ‘summer-birds’ = butterflies. “fieng” = 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Schneeweißchen aber saß daheim bei der Mutter, half ihr im Hauswesen, oder las ihr vor, wenn nichts zu thun war.
sentences.l: Snow-white, however, sat at home with the mother, helped her in the household, or read aloud to her when there was nothing to do.
sentences.i: Snow-white, though, stayed at home with her mother, helped her about the house, or read to her when there was nothing to do.
sentences.n: “vorlesen” — to read aloud (separable); the particle ‘vor’ stands at the end. “thun” = 1857 spelling of tun.

sentences.t: Die beiden Kinder hatten einander so lieb, daß sie sich immer an den Händen faßten, so oft sie zusammen ausgiengen:
sentences.l: The two children held each other so dear that they always took each other by the hands, as often as they went out together:
sentences.i: The two children loved each other so dearly that they always took hands, whenever they went out together:
sentences.n: “einander lieb haben” — to be fond of one another. “ausgiengen” = 1857 spelling of ausgingen (went out), separable.

sentences.t: und wenn Schneeweißchen sagte „wir wollen uns nicht verlassen,“ so antwortete Rosenroth „so lange wir leben nicht,“ und die Mutter setzte hinzu „was das eine hat solls mit dem andern theilen.“
sentences.l: and when Snow-white said, “we will not leave each other,” then Rose-red answered, “not so long as we live,” and the mother added, “what the one has, it shall share with the other.”
sentences.i: and when Snow-white said, “let us never part,” Rose-red would answer, “not as long as we live,” and their mother added, “what one has, she shall share with the other.”
sentences.n: “solls” = soll es; “theilen” = 1857 spelling of teilen (to share). “hinzusetzen” — to add (separable).

sentences.t: Oft liefen sie im Walde allein umher und sammelten rothe Beeren, aber kein Thier that ihnen etwas zu leid, sondern sie kamen vertraulich herbei:
sentences.l: Often they ran about in the wood alone and gathered red berries, but no animal did them any harm; rather they came up trustingly:
sentences.i: Often they roamed the wood alone and gathered red berries, yet no beast did them any harm; instead the creatures came up to them without fear:
sentences.n: “Thier” and “that” keep 1857 spellings (Tier, tat). “einem etwas zu leid thun” — to do someone a hurt. “sondern” = ‘rather, instead,’ after a negative.

sentences.t: das Häschen fraß ein Kohlblatt aus ihren Händen, das Reh graste an ihrer Seite, der Hirsch sprang ganz lustig vorbei und die Vögel blieben auf den Ästen sitzen und sangen was sie nur wußten.
sentences.l: the little hare ate a cabbage-leaf from their hands, the roe grazed at their side, the stag sprang quite merrily past, and the birds stayed sitting on the boughs and sang all they knew.
sentences.i: the little hare ate a cabbage-leaf out of their hands, the roe grazed at their side, the stag bounded merrily by, and the birds stayed perched on the boughs and sang all they knew.
sentences.n: “fraß” is from “fressen” (to eat, of animals), distinct from human ‘essen.’ “was sie nur wußten” — ‘all that they knew,’ i.e. every song they had.

sentences.t: Kein Unfall traf sie:
sentences.l: No mishap befell them:
sentences.n: “treffen” here = to befall, strike. The colon opens the illustration that follows.

sentences.t: wenn sie sich im Walde verspätet hatten und die Nacht sie überfiel, so legten sie sich nebeneinander auf das Moos und schliefen bis der Morgen kam, und die Mutter wußte das und hatte ihrentwegen keine Sorge.
sentences.l: when they had lingered too long in the wood and night came over them, they lay down side by side on the moss and slept until the morning came, and the mother knew this and had no worry on their account.
sentences.i: if they had stayed out too late in the wood and night overtook them, they lay down side by side on the moss and slept till morning came, and their mother knew it and felt no worry for them.
sentences.n: “sich verspäten” — to be late, linger too long. “überfiel” from “überfallen,” here of night ‘coming over’ them. “ihrentwegen” = on their account.

sentences.t: Einmal, als sie im Walde übernachtet hatten und das Morgenroth sie aufweckte, da sahen sie ein schönes Kind in einem weißen glänzenden Kleidchen neben ihrem Lager sitzen.
sentences.l: Once, when they had passed the night in the wood and the red of morning woke them, they saw a beautiful child in a white shining little dress sitting beside their resting-place.
sentences.i: Once, when they had spent the night in the wood and the dawn woke them, they saw a beautiful child in a shining white dress sitting beside where they lay.
sentences.n: “Morgenroth” (1857 spelling) = the red of dawn. “Lager” here = a resting-place, bed of moss.

sentences.t: Es stand auf und blickte sie ganz freundlich an, sprach aber nichts und gieng in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: It stood up and looked at them quite kindly, but said nothing and went off into the wood.
sentences.i: It rose and looked at them very kindly, but said nothing and walked away into the wood.
sentences.n: “Es” (it) because ‘das Kind’ is neuter. “anblicken” — to look at (separable). “gieng” = 1857 spelling of ging.

sentences.t: Und als sie sich umsahen, so hatten sie ganz nahe bei einem Abgrunde geschlafen,
sentences.l: And when they looked about them, they had slept quite close to a chasm,
sentences.i: And when they looked around, they found they had slept right at the edge of a chasm,
sentences.n: “sich umsehen” — to look around (separable). “Abgrund” = abyss, precipice.

sentences.t: und wären gewis hinein gefallen, wenn sie in der Dunkelheit noch ein paar Schritte weiter gegangen wären.
sentences.l: and would surely have fallen in, if they had gone a few steps further in the darkness.
sentences.i: and would surely have fallen in, had they gone a few steps further in the dark.
sentences.n: A contrary-to-fact conditional: “wären … gefallen … wenn … gegangen wären.” “gewis” = 1857 spelling of gewiss.

sentences.t: Die Mutter aber sagte ihnen das müßte der Engel gewesen sein, der gute Kinder bewache.
sentences.l: But the mother told them that must have been the angel who watches over good children.
sentences.i: But their mother told them it must have been the angel who watches over good children.
sentences.n: “müßte … gewesen sein” — subjunctive of inference, ‘must have been.’ “bewache” is subjunctive in the reported clause; “bewachen” = to guard, watch over.

sentences.t: Schneeweißchen und Rosenroth hielten das Hüttchen der Mutter so reinlich, daß es eine Freude war hinein zu schauen.
sentences.l: Snow-white and Rose-red kept the mother’s little cottage so clean that it was a joy to look inside.
sentences.i: Snow-white and Rose-red kept their mother’s little cottage so spotless that it was a joy to look in.
sentences.n: “reinlich” = clean, tidy. “daß” (1857 for dass) opens the result clause.

sentences.t: Im Sommer besorgte Rosenroth das Haus und stellte der Mutter jeden Morgen, ehe sie aufwachte, einen Blumenstrauß vors Bett, darin war von jedem Bäumchen eine Rose.
sentences.l: In summer Rose-red saw to the house and set before the mother every morning, before she awoke, a nosegay by her bed, in which was one rose from each little tree.
sentences.i: In summer Rose-red looked after the house and set a nosegay by her mother’s bed each morning before she woke, with one rose from each little tree in it.
sentences.n: “besorgen” — to see to, take care of. “ehe” = before (conjunction). “vors” = vor das.

sentences.t: Im Winter zündete Schneeweißchen das Feuer an und hieng den Kessel an den Feuerhaken,
sentences.l: In winter Snow-white lit the fire and hung the kettle on the pot-hook,
sentences.i: In winter Snow-white kindled the fire and hung the kettle on the pot-hook,
sentences.n: “anzünden” — to light, kindle (separable, particle an-). “hieng” = 1857 spelling of hing (hung). “Feuerhaken” = the hook the kettle hangs from over the hearth.

sentences.t: und der Kessel war von Messing, glänzte aber wie Gold, so rein war er gescheuert.
sentences.l: and the kettle was of brass, but shone like gold, so clean was it scoured.
sentences.i: and the kettle was of brass, yet shone like gold, it was scoured so clean.
sentences.n: “Messing” here is plain High German ‘brass,’ the metal — not any dialect word the same spelling can carry. “scheuern” — to scour, scrub.

sentences.t: Abends, wenn die Flocken fielen, sagte die Mutter „geh, Schneeweißchen, und schieb den Riegel vor,“
sentences.l: In the evening, when the flakes fell, the mother said, “go, Snow-white, and push the bolt across,”
sentences.i: Of an evening, when the snowflakes fell, their mother would say, “go, Snow-white, and draw the bolt,”
sentences.n: “den Riegel vorschieben” — to push the bolt to, bolt the door (separable, particle vor-). “Flocken” = snowflakes.

sentences.t: und dann setzten sie sich an den Herd, und die Mutter nahm die Brille und las aus einem großen Buche vor, und die beiden Mädchen hörten zu, saßen und spannen;
sentences.l: and then they sat down by the hearth, and the mother took her spectacles and read aloud from a great book, and the two girls listened, sat and spun;
sentences.i: and then they would sit down by the hearth, and their mother would take her spectacles and read aloud from a great book, and the two girls listened, sitting and spinning;
sentences.n: “zuhören” — to listen (separable). “spannen” = spun (from spinnen). “Buche” = dative of Buch with the older -e ending.

sentences.t: neben ihnen lag ein Lämmchen auf dem Boden, und hinter ihnen auf einer Stange saß ein weißes Täubchen und hatte seinen Kopf unter den Flügel gesteckt.
sentences.l: beside them a little lamb lay on the floor, and behind them on a perch sat a white little dove and had put its head under its wing.
sentences.i: beside them a little lamb lay on the floor, and behind them on a perch sat a little white dove with its head tucked under its wing.
sentences.n: “Lämmchen” and “Täubchen” are diminutives (little lamb, little dove). “Stange” here = a pole or perch.

sentences.t: Eines Abends, als sie so vertraulich beisammen saßen, klopfte jemand an die Thüre, als wollte er eingelassen sein.
sentences.l: One evening, as they sat so cosily together, someone knocked at the door, as though he wished to be let in.
sentences.i: One evening, as they sat so snugly together, someone knocked at the door, as if he wanted to be let in.
sentences.n: “eines Abends” is a genitive of time, ‘one evening.’ “Thüre” = 1857 spelling of Türe. “eingelassen sein” — to be admitted.

sentences.t: Die Mutter sprach „geschwind, Rosenroth, mach auf, es wird ein Wanderer sein, der Obdach sucht.“
sentences.l: The mother said, “quick, Rose-red, open up, it will be a wayfarer who is seeking shelter.”
sentences.i: Their mother said, “quick, Rose-red, open the door, it will be some wayfarer looking for shelter.”
sentences.n: “es wird … sein” is a presumptive future, ‘it must be, it will be.’ “aufmachen” — to open (separable). “Obdach” = shelter, a roof for the night.

sentences.t: Rosenroth gieng und schob den Riegel weg und dachte es wäre ein armer Mann,
sentences.l: Rose-red went and pushed the bolt away and thought it was a poor man,
sentences.i: Rose-red went and drew back the bolt, thinking it was some poor man,
sentences.n: “wegschieben” — to push away (separable). “es wäre” is subjunctive of her supposition, ‘that it was.’

sentences.t: aber der war es nicht, es war ein Bär, der seinen dicken schwarzen Kopf zur Thüre herein streckte.
sentences.l: but that it was not; it was a bear, who stretched his thick black head in at the door.
sentences.i: but that it was not; it was a bear, thrusting his thick black head in at the door.
sentences.n: “der war es nicht” — ‘that it was not.’ “hereinstrecken” — to stick in (separable); ‘zur Thüre herein’ = in through the door.

sentences.t: Rosenroth schrie laut und sprang zurück:
sentences.l: Rose-red screamed aloud and sprang back:
sentences.n: “zurückspringen” — to spring back (separable). The colon opens the flurry that follows.

sentences.t: das Lämmchen blöckte, das Täubchen flatterte auf und Schneeweißchen versteckte sich hinter der Mutter Bett.
sentences.l: the little lamb bleated, the little dove fluttered up and Snow-white hid herself behind the mother’s bed.
sentences.i: the little lamb bleated, the dove fluttered up, and Snow-white hid behind her mother’s bed.
sentences.n: “blöcken” — to bleat. “auffliegen/aufflattern” — to flutter up (separable). “der Mutter Bett” is an older genitive without -s, ‘the mother’s bed.’

sentences.t: Der Bär aber fieng an zu sprechen und sagte „fürchtet euch nicht, ich thue euch nichts zu leid, ich bin halb erfroren und will mich nur ein wenig bei euch wärmen.“
sentences.l: But the bear began to speak and said, “do not be afraid, I will do you no harm, I am half frozen and only want to warm myself a little with you.”
sentences.i: But the bear began to speak and said, “don’t be afraid, I’ll do you no harm; I am half frozen and only want to warm myself a little here with you.”
sentences.n: “anfangen” — to begin (separable). “sich fürchten” — to be afraid; “euch” is ‘you’ (plural). “erfroren” from “erfrieren,” to freeze.

sentences.t: „Du armer Bär,“ sprach die Mutter, „leg dich ans Feuer, und gib nur acht daß dir dein Pelz nicht brennt.“
sentences.l: “You poor bear,” said the mother, “lay yourself down by the fire, and only take care that your fur does not burn.”
sentences.i: “You poor bear,” said their mother, “lie down by the fire, and only take care your fur doesn’t catch.”
sentences.n: “du” is rendered ‘you’ throughout — the elevated register comes from cadence, not archaic pronouns. “acht geben” — to take heed, be careful. “ans” = an das.

sentences.t: Dann rief sie „Schneeweißchen, Rosenroth, kommt hervor, der Bär thut euch nichts, er meints ehrlich.“
sentences.l: Then she called, “Snow-white, Rose-red, come out, the bear will do you nothing, he means it honestly.”
sentences.i: Then she called, “Snow-white, Rose-red, come out, the bear won’t hurt you, he means well.”
sentences.n: “hervorkommen” — to come out (separable). “meints” = meint es; “es ehrlich meinen” = to mean it honestly, be sincere.

sentences.t: Da kamen sie beide heran, und nach und nach näherten sich auch das Lämmchen und Täubchen und hatten keine Furcht vor ihm.
sentences.l: Then they both came up, and little by little the little lamb and dove drew near too and had no fear of him.
sentences.i: Then they both came near, and little by little the lamb and dove drew close too and had no fear of him.
sentences.n: “herankommen” — to come up (separable). “sich nähern” + dative — to approach. “nach und nach” = gradually.

sentences.t: Der Bär sprach „ihr Kinder, klopft mir den Schnee ein wenig aus dem Pelzwerk,“ und sie holten den Besen und kehrten dem Bär das Fell rein:
sentences.l: The bear said, “you children, knock the snow a little out of my fur for me,” and they fetched the broom and swept the bear’s coat clean:
sentences.i: The bear said, “children, beat the snow a little out of my fur for me,” and they fetched the broom and swept the bear’s coat clean:
sentences.n: “mir … aus dem Pelzwerk” — dative of interest, ‘for me.’ “kehren” here = to sweep. The colon leads to the bear’s contentment.

sentences.t: er aber streckte sich ans Feuer und brummte ganz vergnügt und behaglich.
sentences.l: but he stretched himself out by the fire and growled quite contentedly and cosily.
sentences.i: but he stretched out by the fire and growled away, quite content and snug.
sentences.n: “sich strecken” — to stretch oneself out. “behaglich” = cosy, comfortable.

sentences.t: Nicht lange, so wurden sie ganz vertraut und trieben Muthwillen mit dem unbeholfenen Gast.
sentences.l: Not long, and they grew quite familiar and made mischief with the clumsy guest.
sentences.i: Before long they grew quite at ease with him and made merry mischief with their clumsy guest.
sentences.n: “Muthwillen treiben” (1857 spelling of Mutwillen) — to be up to mischief, play wantonly. “unbeholfen” = clumsy, ungainly.

sentences.t: Sie zausten ihm das Fell mit den Händen, setzten ihre Füßchen auf seinen Rücken und walgerten ihn hin und her,
sentences.l: They tugged at his coat with their hands, set their little feet on his back and rolled him this way and that,
sentences.i: They tousled his coat with their hands, set their little feet on his back and rolled him to and fro,
sentences.n: “zausen” — to tug, tousle; “ihm das Fell” is dative of the body-part. “walgern” is a dialectal ‘to roll about.’

sentences.t: oder sie nahmen eine Haselruthe und schlugen auf ihn los, und wenn er brummte, so lachten sie.
sentences.l: or they took a hazel switch and beat away at him, and when he growled, they laughed.
sentences.i: or they took a hazel switch and laid into him, and when he growled, they laughed.
sentences.n: “auf jemanden losschlagen” — to beat away at someone (separable). “Haselruthe” = 1857 spelling of Haselrute, a hazel rod.

sentences.t: Der Bär ließ sichs aber gerne gefallen, nur wenn sies gar zu arg machten, rief er „laßt mich am Leben, ihr Kinder:
sentences.l: But the bear gladly put up with it; only when they made it far too rough did he call out, “leave me alive, you children:
sentences.i: But the bear bore it all gladly; only when they went far too far did he cry out, “leave me my life, children:
sentences.n: “sich etwas gefallen lassen” — to put up with something. “sies” = sie es, “sichs” = sich es. “gar zu arg” = far too much. The colon opens the rhymed threat in the next (verse) block.

sentences.t:
Schneeweißchen, Rosenroth,
schlägst dir den Freier todt.“
sentences.l:
Snow-white, Rose-red,
you strike your suitor dead.
sentences.i:
Snow-white, Rose-red,
you’ll beat your suitor to death.
sentences.n: In the text the names stay untranslated; here Schneeweißchen = ‘little Snow-white,’ Rosenroth = ‘Rose-red.’ The German rhymes “Rosenroth” with “todt” (1857 spelling of tot) — a rhyme Lectorium’s plain rendering does not reproduce. “dir” is an ethical dative, roughly ‘you’ll go and strike.’ The bear jokingly calls himself the girls’ “Freier” (suitor).

sentences.t: Als Schlafenszeit war und die andern zu Bett giengen, sagte die Mutter zu dem Bär „du kannst in Gottes Namen da am Herde liegen bleiben, so bist du vor der Kälte und dem bösen Wetter geschützt.“
sentences.l: When it was bedtime and the others went to bed, the mother said to the bear, “you may, in God’s name, stay lying there by the hearth, so you are protected from the cold and the foul weather.”
sentences.i: When bedtime came and the others went to bed, their mother said to the bear, “you may, in God’s name, stay lying there by the hearth; that way you’ll be safe from the cold and the foul weather.”
sentences.n: “giengen” = 1857 spelling of gingen. “in Gottes Namen” = a mild blessing on the permission, ‘by all means.’ “liegen bleiben” — to stay lying.

sentences.t: Sobald der Tag graute, ließen ihn die beiden Kinder hinaus, und er trabte über den Schnee in den Wald hinein.
sentences.l: As soon as the day dawned, the two children let him out, and he trotted over the snow off into the wood.
sentences.i: As soon as day broke, the two children let him out, and he trotted off over the snow into the wood.
sentences.n: “der Tag graut” — the day dawns (grows grey). “hinaus … hinein” mark the directions out and in.

sentences.t: Von nun an kam der Bär jeden Abend zu der bestimmten Stunde, legte sich an den Herd und erlaubte den Kindern Kurzweil mit ihm zu treiben, so viel sie wollten;
sentences.l: From now on the bear came every evening at the appointed hour, laid himself down by the hearth and allowed the children to make sport with him, as much as they liked;
sentences.i: From then on the bear came every evening at the set hour, lay down by the hearth and let the children make sport with him, as much as they liked;
sentences.n: “Kurzweil treiben” — to amuse oneself, make sport (die Kurzweil = pastime, the opposite of Langeweile).

sentences.t: und sie waren so gewöhnt an ihn, daß die Thüre nicht eher zugeriegelt ward, als bis der schwarze Gesell angelangt war.
sentences.l: and they were so used to him that the door was not bolted until the black fellow had arrived.
sentences.i: and they grew so used to him that the door was never bolted until the black fellow had come.
sentences.n: “nicht eher … als bis” — ‘not before … until,’ i.e. not until. “ward” = old past of werden (was); “zugeriegelt” = bolted (separable, zu-). “Gesell” = fellow, companion.

sentences.t: Als das Frühjahr herangekommen und draußen alles grün war, sagte der Bär eines Morgens zu Schneeweißchen „nun muß ich fort und darf den ganzen Sommer nicht wieder kommen.“
sentences.l: When the spring had come on and everything was green outside, the bear said one morning to Snow-white, “now I must be off and may not come again the whole summer through.”
sentences.i: When spring had come and everything was green outdoors, the bear said one morning to Snow-white, “now I must be off, and I may not come again all summer long.”
sentences.n: “herankommen” — to draw near, come on. “fort müssen” — to have to go away; “nicht wieder kommen dürfen” — not be allowed to return.

sentences.t: „Wo gehst du denn hin, lieber Bär?“ fragte Schneeweißchen.
sentences.l: “Where are you going, then, dear bear?” asked Snow-white.
sentences.n: “wohin gehst du?” is split as “wo gehst du … hin,” the ‘hin’ landing at the end — normal spoken order. “denn” softens the question.

sentences.t: „Ich muß in den Wald und meine Schätze vor den bösen Zwergen hüten:
sentences.l: “I must into the wood and guard my treasures from the wicked dwarfs:
sentences.i: “I must go into the wood and guard my treasures from the wicked dwarfs:
sentences.n: “etwas vor jemandem hüten” — to guard something against someone. A verb of motion (‘go’) is understood after “muß in den Wald.”

sentences.t: im Winter, wenn die Erde hart gefroren ist, müssen sie wohl unten bleiben und können sich nicht durcharbeiten, aber jetzt, wenn die Sonne die Erde aufgethaut und erwärmt hat, da brechen sie durch, steigen herauf, suchen und stehlen;
sentences.l: in winter, when the earth is frozen hard, they must indeed stay below and cannot work their way through, but now, when the sun has thawed and warmed the earth, they break through, climb up, search and steal;
sentences.i: in winter, when the earth is frozen hard, they must stay down below and cannot dig their way up; but now, once the sun has thawed and warmed the earth, they break through, climb up, and go searching and stealing;
sentences.n: “aufgethaut” = 1857 spelling of aufgetaut. “durcharbeiten” / “durchbrechen” — to work / break through (separable). “wohl” here = ‘indeed, admittedly.’

sentences.t: was einmal in ihren Händen ist und in ihren Höhlen liegt, das kommt so leicht nicht wieder an des Tages Licht.“
sentences.l: what is once in their hands and lies in their caves, that does not come again so easily to the light of day.”
sentences.i: whatever is once in their hands and lies in their caves does not come to the light of day again so easily.”
sentences.n: “was … das” — the fronted ‘what’ is picked up by ‘das.’ “an des Tages Licht” = to the light of day, a genitive before its noun.

sentences.t: Schneeweißchen war ganz traurig über den Abschied und als es ihm die Thüre aufriegelte, und der Bär sich hinaus drängte, blieb er an dem Thürhaken hängen und ein Stück seiner Haut riß auf, und da war es Schneeweißchen, als hätte es Gold durchschimmern gesehen:
sentences.l: Snow-white was quite sad at the parting, and as she unbolted the door for him, and the bear pressed his way out, he caught on the door-hook and a piece of his skin tore open, and then it seemed to Snow-white as if she had seen gold shimmer through:
sentences.i: Snow-white was very sad at the parting, and as she unbolted the door for him and the bear pushed his way out, he caught on the door-hook and a piece of his hide tore open, and then it seemed to Snow-white as though she had glimpsed gold shimmering through:
sentences.n: “es” for Snow-white because ‘das Schneeweißchen’ is neuter — rendered ‘she.’ “aufriegeln” — to unbolt. “es war ihm, als hätte …” — ‘it seemed to her as if she had …,’ subjunctive.

sentences.t: aber es war seiner Sache nicht gewis.
sentences.l: but she was not sure of the matter.
sentences.i: but she could not be sure of it.
sentences.n: “seiner Sache gewis sein” (1857 gewis = gewiss) — to be sure of one’s ground, certain. “seiner” refers back to neuter Schneeweißchen.

sentences.t: Der Bär lief eilig fort und war bald hinter den Bäumen verschwunden.
sentences.l: The bear ran hastily away and was soon vanished behind the trees.
sentences.i: The bear ran off in haste and was soon lost to sight behind the trees.
sentences.n: “fortlaufen” — to run away (separable). “eilig” = hurried, in haste.

sentences.t: Nach einiger Zeit schickte die Mutter die Kinder in den Wald, Reisig zu sammeln.
sentences.l: After some time the mother sent the children into the wood to gather brushwood.
sentences.i: After a while their mother sent the children into the wood to gather kindling.
sentences.n: “Reisig” = brushwood, twigs for the fire. The bare infinitive “zu sammeln” gives the purpose, ‘to gather.’

sentences.t: Da fanden sie draußen einen großen Baum, der lag gefällt auf dem Boden,
sentences.l: There they found out of doors a great tree, which lay felled upon the ground,
sentences.i: There they came upon a great tree lying felled on the ground,
sentences.n: “der lag …” picks the tree up with a resumptive ‘which,’ common in older German. “gefällt” = felled, cut down.

sentences.t: und an dem Stamme sprang zwischen dem Gras etwas auf und ab, sie konnten aber nicht unterscheiden was es war.
sentences.l: and by the trunk something sprang up and down among the grass, but they could not make out what it was.
sentences.i: and by the trunk something was jumping up and down among the grass, but they could not tell what it was.
sentences.n: “auf und ab” — up and down. “unterscheiden” here = to make out, distinguish. “Stamme” = dative of Stamm with older -e.

sentences.t: Als sie näher kamen, sahen sie einen Zwerg mit einem alten verwelkten Gesicht und einem ellenlangen schneeweißen Bart.
sentences.l: When they came nearer, they saw a dwarf with an old withered face and a beard an ell long, snow-white.
sentences.i: As they came nearer, they saw a dwarf with an old, withered face and a snow-white beard an ell long.
sentences.n: “ellenlang” — an ‘ell’ long, i.e. very long (die Elle, an old measure of roughly two feet). “verwelkt” = withered.

sentences.t: Das Ende des Bartes war in eine Spalte des Baums eingeklemmt,
sentences.l: The end of the beard was wedged into a cleft of the tree,
sentences.i: The end of the beard was jammed into a crack in the tree,
sentences.n: “einklemmen” — to wedge in, pinch (separable). “Spalte” = cleft, crack.

sentences.t: und der Kleine sprang hin und her wie ein Hündchen an einem Seil und wußte nicht wie er sich helfen sollte.
sentences.l: and the little one sprang to and fro like a little dog on a rope and did not know how he should help himself.
sentences.i: and the little fellow leapt to and fro like a puppy on a rope and did not know how to help himself.
sentences.n: “der Kleine” — ‘the little one,’ adjective used as a noun. “sich helfen” — to help oneself, manage.

sentences.t: Er glotzte die Mädchen mit seinen rothen feurigen Augen an und schrie „was steht ihr da! könnt ihr nicht herbei gehen und mir Beistand leisten?“
sentences.l: He goggled at the girls with his red fiery eyes and screamed, “what are you standing there for! can you not come over and lend me aid?”
sentences.i: He goggled at the girls with his red, fiery eyes and screamed, “what are you standing there for! can’t you come over and lend me a hand?”
sentences.n: “anglotzen” — to stare, goggle at (separable). “Beistand leisten” — to render assistance. “rothen” = 1857 spelling of roten.

sentences.t: „Was hast du angefangen, kleines Männchen?“ fragte Rosenroth.
sentences.l: “What have you begun, little manikin?” asked Rose-red.
sentences.i: “What have you got yourself into, little manikin?” asked Rose-red.
sentences.n: “was hast du angefangen?” — literally ‘what have you started,’ i.e. what have you been up to. “Männchen” = little man, manikin.

sentences.t: „Dumme neugierige Gans,“ antwortete der Zwerg, „den Baum habe ich mir spalten wollen, um kleines Holz in der Küche zu haben;
sentences.l: “Stupid, inquisitive goose,” answered the dwarf, “I meant to split myself the tree, so as to have small wood in the kitchen;
sentences.i: “Stupid, prying goose,” answered the dwarf, “I meant to split the tree for myself, to have small wood for the kitchen;
sentences.n: “mir … spalten wollen” — ‘to have meant to split for myself,’ dative of interest. “um … zu haben” = in order to have. “Gans” (goose) as an insult, ‘silly goose.’

sentences.t: bei den dicken Klötzen verbrennt gleich das bischen Speise, das unser einer braucht, der nicht so viel hinunter schlingt als ihr, grobes, gieriges Volk.
sentences.l: with the thick logs the little bit of food burns up at once that the likes of us needs, who does not gulp down so much as you, coarse, greedy rabble.
sentences.i: over thick logs the little bit of food burns up straight away that the likes of us needs — who does not gulp down as much as you do, you coarse, greedy rabble.
sentences.n: “Volk” here is plain High German ‘folk,’ used scornfully as ‘rabble, lot’ — not a dialect word. “unser einer” — ‘one of us, the likes of us.’ “bischen” = 1857 spelling of bisschen.

sentences.t: Ich hatte den Keil schon glücklich hinein getrieben, und es wäre alles nach Wunsch gegangen, aber das verwünschte Holz war zu glatt und sprang unversehens heraus, und der Baum fuhr so geschwind zusammen, daß ich meinen schönen weißen Bart nicht mehr herausziehen konnte;
sentences.l: I had already driven the wedge in nicely, and all would have gone as I wished, but the accursed wood was too smooth and sprang out unexpectedly, and the tree snapped together so quickly that I could no longer pull out my fine white beard;
sentences.i: I had already driven the wedge in nicely, and all would have gone as I wished, but the cursed wood was too smooth and sprang out all at once, and the tree closed up so fast that I could no longer pull my fine white beard free;
sentences.n: “hineintreiben” / “herausspringen” / “zusammenfahren” — all separable verbs of motion (drive in, spring out, snap together). “unversehens” = unexpectedly, all at once. “verwünscht” = accursed.

sentences.t: nun steckt er drinn, und ich kann nicht fort.
sentences.l: now it is stuck in there, and I cannot get away.
sentences.i: now it’s stuck fast in there, and I can’t get free.
sentences.n: “stecken” — to be stuck. “drinn” = 1857 spelling of drin (in there). “nicht fort können” — to be unable to get away.

sentences.t: Da lachen die albernen glatten Milchgesichter!
sentences.l: There the silly smooth milk-faces laugh!
sentences.i: And there the silly, smooth-cheeked milksops laugh!
sentences.n: “Milchgesicht” (milk-face) is a jeer at a smooth, beardless young face — a milksop. “albern” = silly.

sentences.t: pfui, was seid ihr garstig!“
sentences.l: fie, how nasty you are!”
sentences.i: ugh, how horrid you are!”
sentences.n: “pfui” — an exclamation of disgust, ‘fie, ugh.’ “was” here = ‘how’ in an exclamation. “garstig” = nasty, horrid.

sentences.t: Die Kinder gaben sich alle Mühe, aber sie konnten den Bart nicht heraus ziehen, er steckte zu fest.
sentences.l: The children took all pains, but they could not pull the beard out; it was stuck too fast.
sentences.i: The children tried their hardest, but they could not pull the beard out; it was wedged too fast.
sentences.n: “sich Mühe geben” — to take pains, try hard. “herausziehen” — to pull out (separable).

sentences.t: „Ich will laufen und Leute herbei holen“ sagte Rosenroth.
sentences.l: “I will run and fetch people here,” said Rose-red.
sentences.i: “I’ll run and fetch some people,” said Rose-red.
sentences.n: “herbeiholen” — to fetch, bring here (separable). “wollen” here = ‘to intend, will.’

sentences.t: „Wahnsinnige Schafsköpfe,“ schnarrte der Zwerg, „wer wird gleich Leute herbeirufen, ihr seid mir schon um zwei zu viel;
sentences.l: “Mad blockheads,” snarled the dwarf, “who would go calling people over at once — you are already two too many for me;
sentences.i: “You mad blockheads,” the dwarf snarled, “who calls in people straight off — you are already two too many for me;
sentences.n: “Schafskopf” (sheep’s head) = blockhead. “mir … zu viel” — dative, ‘too many for me.’ “gleich” here = ‘right away, at once.’

sentences.t: fällt euch nicht besseres ein?“
sentences.l: does nothing better occur to you?”
sentences.i: can you think of nothing better?”
sentences.n: “einfallen” — to occur to one (separable), with the dative “euch.” ‘Does nothing better come to your minds?’

sentences.t: „Sei nur nicht ungeduldig,“ sagte Schneeweißchen, „ich will schon Rath schaffen,“ holte sein Scheerchen aus der Tasche und schnitt das Ende des Bartes ab.
sentences.l: “Only do not be impatient,” said Snow-white, “I will manage to find a remedy,” drew her little scissors from her pocket and cut off the end of the beard.
sentences.i: “Now don’t be impatient,” said Snow-white, “I’ll find a way,” drew her little scissors from her pocket and snipped off the end of the beard.
sentences.n: “Rath schaffen” (1857 for Rat schaffen) — to find a remedy, sort things out. “schon” here reassures, ‘I’ll manage all right.’ “Scheerchen” = little scissors; “sein” (its) refers to neuter Schneeweißchen, rendered ‘her.’

sentences.t: Sobald der Zwerg sich frei fühlte, griff er nach einem Sack, der zwischen den Wurzeln des Baums steckte und mit Gold gefüllt war,
sentences.l: As soon as the dwarf felt himself free, he snatched at a sack that was stuck between the roots of the tree and was filled with gold,
sentences.i: The moment the dwarf felt himself free, he grabbed for a sack that was lodged among the roots of the tree, filled with gold,
sentences.n: “nach etwas greifen” — to reach, grab for something. “stecken” here = to be lodged, stuck.

sentences.t: hob ihn heraus und brummte vor sich hin „ungehobeltes Volk, schneidet mir ein Stück von meinem stolzen Barte ab! lohns euch der Guckuck!“
sentences.l: heaved it out and growled to himself, “uncouth rabble, to cut me off a piece of my proud beard! may the cuckoo repay you for it!”
sentences.i: heaved it out and muttered to himself, “uncouth rabble, cutting off a piece of my proud beard! may the cuckoo pay you for it!”
sentences.n: “vor sich hin brummen” — to mutter to oneself. “lohn’s euch der Guckuck” (Guckuck = 1857 Kuckuck) is a grumbling curse, ‘may the cuckoo reward you,’ i.e. bad luck to you. “Volk” again = ‘rabble, lot.’

sentences.t: damit schwang er seinen Sack auf den Rücken und gieng fort ohne die Kinder nur noch einmal anzusehen.
sentences.l: with that he swung his sack onto his back and went off without so much as looking at the children one more time.
sentences.i: with that he swung his sack onto his back and went off without so much as glancing at the children again.
sentences.n: “nur noch einmal” — ‘even once more.’ “ansehen” — to look at (separable), here in the infinitive “anzusehen.”

sentences.t: Einige Zeit danach wollten Schneeweißchen und Rosenroth ein Gericht Fische angeln.
sentences.l: Some time after this, Snow-white and Rose-red wanted to angle a dish of fish.
sentences.i: Some time later, Snow-white and Rose-red wanted to catch a dish of fish.
sentences.n: “ein Gericht Fische” — a dish, a serving of fish. “angeln” = to angle, fish with a line.

sentences.t: Als sie nahe bei dem Bach waren, sahen sie daß etwas wie eine große Heuschrecke nach dem Wasser zu hüpfte, als wollte es hinein springen.
sentences.l: When they were near the brook, they saw that something like a great grasshopper was hopping towards the water, as if it wanted to spring in.
sentences.i: When they were near the brook, they saw something like a great grasshopper hopping toward the water, as if it meant to leap in.
sentences.n: “nach dem Wasser zu” — toward the water. “als wollte es” — subjunctive, ‘as if it wanted.’ “Heuschrecke” = grasshopper, locust.

sentences.t: Sie liefen heran und erkannten den Zwerg.
sentences.l: They ran up and recognized the dwarf.
sentences.n: “heranlaufen” — to run up (separable). “erkennen” — to recognize.

sentences.t: „Wo willst du hin?“ sagte Rosenroth, „du willst doch nicht ins Wasser?“
sentences.l: “Where are you off to?” said Rose-red, “surely you don’t mean to go into the water?”
sentences.i: “Where are you off to?” said Rose-red, “you don’t mean to go into the water, surely?”
sentences.n: “wo willst du hin?” — ‘where do you want to go,’ with ‘hin’ at the end. “doch nicht” expects the answer ‘no,’ ‘surely not.’

sentences.t: „Solch ein Narr bin ich nicht,“ schrie der Zwerg, „seht ihr nicht, der verwünschte Fisch will mich hinein ziehen?“
sentences.l: “Such a fool I am not,” screamed the dwarf, “do you not see, the accursed fish wants to pull me in?”
sentences.i: “I’m no such fool,” screamed the dwarf, “can’t you see, the cursed fish is trying to drag me in?”
sentences.n: “solch ein Narr” — such a fool. “hineinziehen” — to pull in (separable). “verwünscht” = accursed.

sentences.t: Der Kleine hatte da gesessen und geangelt, und unglücklicher Weise hatte der Wind seinen Bart mit der Angelschnur verflochten:
sentences.l: The little one had sat there and angled, and unluckily the wind had entwined his beard with the fishing-line:
sentences.i: The little fellow had been sitting there fishing, and by ill luck the wind had tangled his beard up with the fishing-line:
sentences.n: “unglücklicher Weise” (now written unglücklicherweise) — unluckily. “verflechten” — to interweave, entangle. “Angelschnur” = fishing-line.

sentences.t: als gleich darauf ein großer Fisch anbiß, fehlten dem schwachen Geschöpf die Kräfte ihn herauszuziehen:
sentences.l: when straight after a big fish bit, the weak creature lacked the strength to pull it out:
sentences.i: when a big fish bit a moment later, the weak creature lacked the strength to haul it out:
sentences.n: “anbeißen” — to bite (of a fish taking the bait; separable). “dem … Geschöpf … die Kräfte” — dative, ‘the creature lacked the strength.’

sentences.t: der Fisch behielt die Oberhand und riß den Zwerg zu sich hin.
sentences.l: the fish kept the upper hand and dragged the dwarf towards itself.
sentences.i: the fish kept the upper hand and dragged the dwarf toward it.
sentences.n: “die Oberhand behalten” — to keep the upper hand. “zu sich hin reißen” — to pull toward oneself (separable).

sentences.t: Zwar hielt er sich an allen Halmen und Binsen, aber das half nicht viel, er mußte den Bewegungen des Fisches folgen, und war in beständiger Gefahr ins Wasser gezogen zu werden.
sentences.l: True, he held on to all the stalks and rushes, but that helped little; he had to follow the movements of the fish, and was in constant danger of being drawn into the water.
sentences.i: He clung, true enough, to every stalk and rush, but it helped little; he had to follow the fish’s movements, and was in constant danger of being pulled into the water.
sentences.n: “zwar … aber” — ‘it is true … but,’ a concession. “den Bewegungen folgen” — to follow the movements (dative). “gezogen zu werden” = passive infinitive, ‘to be drawn.’

sentences.t: Die Mädchen kamen zu rechter Zeit, hielten ihn fest und versuchten den Bart von der Schnur loszumachen,
sentences.l: The girls came at the right time, held him fast and tried to loosen the beard from the line,
sentences.i: The girls came just in time, held him fast and tried to free his beard from the line,
sentences.n: “zu rechter Zeit” — at the right time, just in time. “losmachen” — to loosen, free (separable, particle los-).

sentences.t: aber vergebens, Bart und Schnur waren fest in einander verwirrt.
sentences.l: but in vain; beard and line were fast tangled into one another.
sentences.i: but in vain; beard and line were tangled tight together.
sentences.n: “vergebens” — in vain. “in einander verwirrt” — tangled into one another.

sentences.t: Es blieb nichts übrig als das Scheerchen hervor zu holen und den Bart abzuschneiden, wobei ein kleiner Theil desselben verloren gieng.
sentences.l: Nothing remained but to bring out the little scissors and cut off the beard, whereby a small part of it was lost.
sentences.i: There was nothing for it but to bring out the little scissors and cut the beard, and in doing so a small part of it was lost.
sentences.n: “es bleibt nichts übrig als” — there is nothing left but to. “Theil” / “gieng” = 1857 spellings of Teil, ging. “desselben” = of it (the beard).

sentences.t: Als der Zwerg das sah, schrie er sie an, „ist das Manier, ihr Lorche, einem das Gesicht zu schänden?
sentences.l: When the dwarf saw this, he screamed at them, “is that any manners, you louts, to disfigure a person’s face?
sentences.i: When the dwarf saw this, he screamed at them, “is that any way to behave, you louts, disfiguring a person’s face?
sentences.n: “anschreien” — to shout at (separable). “ist das Manier?” — ‘is that good manners?’ “Lorche” is a term of abuse, roughly ‘clumsy louts’ (sense uncertain). “einem” = ‘to one, to a person.’

sentences.t: nicht genug, daß ihr mir den Bart unten abgestutzt habt, jetzt schneidet ihr mir den besten Theil davon ab:
sentences.l: not enough that you have clipped my beard off below, now you cut the best part of it off for me:
sentences.i: as if it were not enough that you clipped my beard off at the bottom, now you cut off the best part of it:
sentences.n: “nicht genug, daß …” — ‘not content that …, as if it weren’t enough that.’ “abstutzen” / “abschneiden” — to clip / cut off (separable). “mir” is dative, of the wronged party.

sentences.t: ich darf mich vor den Meinigen gar nicht sehen lassen.
sentences.l: I dare not show myself at all before my own people.
sentences.i: I can’t let myself be seen at all before my own folk.
sentences.n: “sich sehen lassen” — to let oneself be seen, show oneself. “die Meinigen” — my own people, my kin.

sentences.t: Daß ihr laufen müßtet und die Schuhsohlen verloren hättet!“
sentences.l: May you have to run and lose the soles of your shoes!”
sentences.i: May you run till the very soles fall off your shoes!”
sentences.n: A curse in the subjunctive: “daß ihr … müßtet … hättet!” — ‘would that you had to …,’ wishing them ill. “müßtet” = 1857 spelling of müsstet.

sentences.t: Dann holte er einen Sack Perlen, der im Schilfe lag, und ohne ein Wort weiter zu sagen, schleppte er ihn fort und verschwand hinter einem Stein.
sentences.l: Then he fetched a sack of pearls that lay in the reeds, and without saying a word more, he dragged it off and vanished behind a stone.
sentences.i: Then he fetched a sack of pearls that lay in the reeds and, without another word, dragged it off and disappeared behind a stone.
sentences.n: “Schilf” = reeds, sedge; “im Schilfe” with older dative -e. “fortschleppen” — to drag away (separable).

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß bald hernach die Mutter die beiden Mädchen nach der Stadt schickte, Zwirn Nadeln Schnüre und Bänder einzukaufen.
sentences.l: It came about that soon after, the mother sent the two girls to the town to buy thread, needles, cords and ribbons.
sentences.i: It came about that, soon after, their mother sent the two girls to town to buy thread, needles, laces and ribbons.
sentences.n: “es trug sich zu” — it came to pass, it happened. The list “Zwirn Nadeln Schnüre und Bänder” stands without commas, as in the source. “einkaufen” — to buy (separable), infinitive with zu.

sentences.t: Der Weg führte sie über eine Heide, auf der hier und da mächtige Felsenstücke zerstreut lagen.
sentences.l: The way led them over a heath, on which here and there mighty chunks of rock lay scattered.
sentences.i: Their way led them across a heath, where great chunks of rock lay scattered here and there.
sentences.n: “hier und da” — here and there. “zerstreut” = scattered, strewn. “Felsenstück” = a piece, chunk of rock.

sentences.t: Da sahen sie einen großen Vogel in der Luft schweben, der langsam über ihnen kreiste, sich immer tiefer herab senkte und endlich nicht weit bei einem Felsen niederstieß.
sentences.l: There they saw a great bird hovering in the air, which slowly circled above them, sank down ever lower and at last swooped down not far off by a rock.
sentences.i: There they saw a great bird hovering in the air, which slowly wheeled above them, sank lower and lower, and at last swooped down not far off beside a rock.
sentences.n: “schweben” — to hover, float. “sich herabsenken” / “niederstoßen” — to sink down / swoop down (separable). “immer tiefer” — ever lower.

sentences.t: Gleich darauf hörten sie einen durchdringenden, jämmerlichen Schrei.
sentences.l: Immediately after, they heard a piercing, pitiful cry.
sentences.i: The next moment they heard a piercing, pitiful cry.
sentences.n: “gleich darauf” — immediately afterwards. “durchdringend” = piercing; “jämmerlich” = pitiful, wretched.

sentences.t: Sie liefen herzu und sahen mit Schrecken daß der Adler ihren alten Bekannten, den Zwerg, gepackt hatte und ihn forttragen wollte.
sentences.l: They ran up and saw with fright that the eagle had seized their old acquaintance, the dwarf, and meant to carry him off.
sentences.i: They ran up and saw to their horror that the eagle had seized their old acquaintance, the dwarf, and was about to carry him off.
sentences.n: “herzulaufen” — to run up (separable). “mit Schrecken” — with fright, in horror. “forttragen” — to carry off (separable).

sentences.t: Die mitleidigen Kinder hielten gleich das Männchen fest und zerrten sich so lange mit dem Adler herum, bis er seine Beute fahren ließ.
sentences.l: The compassionate children at once held the manikin fast and tugged away with the eagle so long, until it let its prey go.
sentences.i: The tender-hearted children at once held the manikin fast and tussled with the eagle until it let go of its prey.
sentences.n: “mitleidig” — compassionate, pitying. “sich herumzerren mit” — to tussle, wrestle with. “fahren lassen” — to let go, release.

sentences.t: Als der Zwerg sich von dem ersten Schrecken erholt hatte, schrie er mit seiner kreischenden Stimme „konntet ihr nicht säuberlicher mit mir umgehen?
sentences.l: When the dwarf had recovered from the first fright, he screamed in his screeching voice, “could you not deal more carefully with me?
sentences.i: When the dwarf had got over his first fright, he screamed in his screeching voice, “could you not have handled me more gently?
sentences.n: “sich erholen von” — to recover from. “mit jemandem umgehen” — to deal with, treat someone. “säuberlicher” = more carefully, more gently.

sentences.t: gerissen habt ihr an meinem dünnen Röckchen daß es überall zerfetzt und durchlöchert ist, unbeholfenes und täppisches Gesindel, das ihr seid!“
sentences.l: you have torn at my thin little coat so that it is ragged and full of holes all over, clumsy and awkward rabble that you are!”
sentences.i: you have torn at my thin little coat till it is ragged and riddled with holes all over — clumsy, blundering rabble that you are!”
sentences.n: “an etwas reißen” — to tear, pull at something. “durchlöchert” = riddled with holes. “Gesindel” = rabble, riffraff; “das ihr seid” = ‘that you are.’

sentences.t: Dann nahm er einen Sack mit Edelsteinen und schlüpfte wieder unter den Felsen in seine Höhle.
sentences.l: Then he took a sack of precious stones and slipped again under the rock into his cave.
sentences.i: Then he took a sack of precious stones and slipped back under the rock into his cave.
sentences.n: “Edelstein” = precious stone, jewel. “schlüpfen” — to slip. “wieder” = again, back.

sentences.t: Die Mädchen waren an seinen Undank schon gewöhnt, setzten ihren Weg fort und verrichteten ihr Geschäft in der Stadt.
sentences.l: The girls were already used to his ingratitude, continued their way and carried out their business in the town.
sentences.i: The girls were used to his ingratitude by now; they went on their way and did their errands in the town.
sentences.n: “an etwas gewöhnt sein” — to be used to something. “Undank” = ingratitude. “fortsetzen” — to continue (separable); “verrichten” = to carry out, perform.

sentences.t: Als sie beim Heimweg wieder auf die Heide kamen, überraschten sie den Zwerg, der auf einem reinlichen Plätzchen seinen Sack mit Edelsteinen ausgeschüttet und nicht gedacht hatte daß so spät noch jemand daher kommen würde.
sentences.l: When on the way home they came again onto the heath, they surprised the dwarf, who on a clean little spot had poured out his sack of precious stones and had not thought that so late anyone would still come along.
sentences.i: On the way home, when they came onto the heath again, they took the dwarf by surprise: on a clean little patch he had tipped out his sack of jewels, never thinking that anyone would still come by so late.
sentences.n: “überraschen” — to surprise, come upon. “ausschütten” — to pour out, tip out (separable). “daherkommen” — to come along (separable).

sentences.t: Die Abendsonne schien über die glänzenden Steine,
sentences.l: The evening sun shone over the glittering stones,
sentences.i: The evening sun shone across the glittering stones,
sentences.n: “Abendsonne” = the evening sun. “glänzend” = gleaming, glittering.

sentences.t: sie schimmerten und leuchteten so prächtig in allen Farben, daß die Kinder stehenblieben und sie betrachteten.
sentences.l: they shimmered and glowed so splendidly in all colours that the children stood still and gazed at them.
sentences.i: they shimmered and glowed so splendidly in every colour that the children stopped and gazed at them.
sentences.n: “stehenbleiben” — to stop, stand still (separable). “betrachten” — to look at, contemplate. “prächtig” = splendid, magnificent.

sentences.t: „Was steht ihr da und habt Maulaffen feil!“ schrie der Zwerg, und sein aschgraues Gesicht ward zinnoberroth vor Zorn.
sentences.l: “What are you standing there for, gaping like fools!” screamed the dwarf, and his ash-grey face turned vermilion with rage.
sentences.i: “What are you standing there for, gaping like fools!” screamed the dwarf, and his ash-grey face turned scarlet with rage.
sentences.n: “Maulaffen feil haben” is a fixed idiom, literally ‘to have gaping-mouths for sale,’ i.e. to stand about idly gawking. “ward” = old past of werden (turned); “zinnoberroth” = vermilion.

sentences.t: Er wollte mit seinen Scheltworten fortfahren, als sich ein lautes Brummen hören ließ und ein schwarzer Bär aus dem Walde herbei trabte.
sentences.l: He was about to go on with his scolding words, when a loud growling made itself heard and a black bear came trotting up out of the wood.
sentences.i: He was about to go on scolding, when a loud growl made itself heard and a black bear came trotting up out of the wood.
sentences.n: “fortfahren” — to continue (separable). “sich hören lassen” — to make itself heard. “Scheltworte” = scolding words, abuse.

sentences.t: Erschrocken sprang der Zwerg auf, aber er konnte nicht mehr zu seinem Schlupfwinkel gelangen, der Bär war schon in seiner Nähe.
sentences.l: Startled, the dwarf sprang up, but he could no longer reach his hiding-hole; the bear was already close to him.
sentences.i: Startled, the dwarf sprang up, but could no longer reach his hiding-hole; the bear was already close by.
sentences.n: “erschrocken” = startled, terrified. “aufspringen” — to spring up (separable). “Schlupfwinkel” = hiding-place, lurking-hole; “gelangen zu” = to reach.

sentences.t: Da rief er in Herzensangst „lieber Herr Bär, verschont mich, ich will euch alle meine Schätze geben, sehet, die schönen Edelsteine, die da liegen.
sentences.l: Then he cried in heart’s anguish, “dear Mister Bear, spare me, I will give you all my treasures, look, the beautiful precious stones that lie there.
sentences.i: Then he cried out in mortal terror, “dear Mister Bear, spare me, I’ll give you all my treasures — look, the fine jewels lying there.
sentences.n: “Herzensangst” = anguish of the heart, mortal terror. “verschonen” — to spare. “sehet” is an older imperative, ‘behold, look.’ He switches to the respectful “euch” (you) with the bear.

sentences.t: Schenkt mir das Leben, was habt ihr an mir kleinen schmächtigen Kerl?
sentences.l: Grant me my life — what have you in me, a small slight fellow?
sentences.i: Spare my life — what use am I to you, a small slight fellow?
sentences.n: “jemandem das Leben schenken” — to grant, spare someone’s life. “was habt ihr an mir?” — ‘what do you get out of me, what use am I to you?’ “schmächtig” = slight, scrawny.

sentences.t: ihr spürt mich nicht zwischen den Zähnen:
sentences.l: you would not feel me between your teeth:
sentences.i: you’d not even feel me between your teeth:
sentences.n: “spüren” — to feel, sense. The colon opens his treacherous suggestion of the girls instead.

sentences.t: da, die beiden gottlosen Mädchen packt, das sind für euch zarte Bissen, fett wie junge Wachteln, die freßt in Gottes Namen.“
sentences.l: there, seize the two godless girls — those are tender morsels for you, fat as young quails; eat them, in God’s name.”
sentences.i: there, take the two godless girls — those are tender morsels for you, plump as young quails; eat them, in God’s name.”
sentences.n: “packt” / “freßt” — imperatives (seize; devour). “fressen” is ‘to eat’ of animals, here of the bear. “Bissen” = morsel, mouthful; “Wachteln” = quails.

sentences.t: Der Bär kümmerte sich um seine Worte nicht, gab dem boshaften Geschöpf einen einzigen Schlag mit der Tatze, und es regte sich nicht mehr.
sentences.l: The bear did not concern himself with his words, gave the malicious creature a single blow with his paw, and it stirred no more.
sentences.i: The bear paid no heed to his words, gave the malicious creature a single blow with his paw, and it stirred no more.
sentences.n: “sich um etwas kümmern” — to concern oneself with, mind. “boshaft” = malicious, spiteful. “sich regen” — to stir, move.

sentences.t: Die Mädchen waren fortgesprungen, aber der Bär rief ihnen nach „Schneeweißchen und Rosenroth, fürchtet euch nicht, wartet ich will mit euch gehen.“
sentences.l: The girls had sprung away, but the bear called after them, “Snow-white and Rose-red, do not be afraid, wait, I will go with you.”
sentences.i: The girls had run off, but the bear called after them, “Snow-white and Rose-red, don’t be afraid, wait, I’ll come with you.”
sentences.n: “fortspringen” — to spring away (separable). “nachrufen” — to call after (separable). “sich fürchten” — to be afraid.

sentences.t: Da erkannten sie seine Stimme und blieben stehen,
sentences.l: Then they recognized his voice and stood still,
sentences.i: Then they knew his voice and stopped,
sentences.n: “erkennen” — to recognize. “stehenbleiben” — to stop, stand still (separable).

sentences.t: und als der Bär bei ihnen war, fiel plötzlich die Bärenhaut ab, und er stand da als ein schöner Mann, und war ganz in Gold gekleidet.
sentences.l: and when the bear was beside them, the bear-skin suddenly fell off, and he stood there as a handsome man, and was clothed all in gold.
sentences.i: and when the bear reached them, the bear-skin suddenly fell away, and he stood there a handsome man, clothed all in gold.
sentences.n: “abfallen” — to fall off (separable). “gekleidet” = clothed, dressed. “ganz in Gold” — all in gold.

sentences.t: „Ich bin eines Königs Sohn,“ sprach er, „und war von dem gottlosen Zwerg, der mir meine Schätze gestohlen hatte, verwünscht als ein wilder Bär in dem Walde zu laufen, bis ich durch seinen Tod erlöst würde.
sentences.l: “I am a king’s son,” he said, “and was cursed by the godless dwarf, who had stolen my treasures from me, to run in the wood as a wild bear, until I should be redeemed by his death.
sentences.i: “I am a king’s son,” he said, “and was put under a spell by the godless dwarf, who had stolen my treasures, to roam the wood as a wild bear until his death should set me free.
sentences.n: “eines Königs Sohn” — a king’s son (genitive before the noun). “verwünscht … zu laufen” — cursed, enchanted to run. “erlöst würde” = subjunctive, ‘should be released.’

sentences.t: Jetzt hat er seine wohlverdiente Strafe empfangen.“
sentences.l: Now he has received his well-deserved punishment.”
sentences.i: Now he has met his well-deserved punishment.”
sentences.n: “wohlverdient” = well-deserved. “Strafe empfangen” — to receive one’s punishment.

sentences.t: Schneeweißchen ward mit ihm vermählt und Rosenroth mit seinem Bruder und sie theilten die großen Schätze mit einander, die der Zwerg in seine Höhle zusammen getragen hatte.
sentences.l: Snow-white was wedded to him and Rose-red to his brother, and they shared the great treasures with one another that the dwarf had gathered together into his cave.
sentences.i: Snow-white was married to him and Rose-red to his brother, and they shared between them the great treasures the dwarf had gathered into his cave.
sentences.n: “ward vermählt” — was wedded (ward = old past of werden). “theilten” = 1857 spelling of teilten. “zusammentragen” — to gather together (separable).

sentences.t: Die alte Mutter lebte noch lange Jahre ruhig und glücklich bei ihren Kindern.
sentences.l: The old mother lived on for many long years, calm and happy, with her children.
sentences.i: The old mother lived on many long years, quiet and happy, with her children.
sentences.n: “noch lange Jahre” — for many years yet. “bei ihren Kindern” — with, at the home of her children.

sentences.t: Die zwei Rosenbäumchen aber nahm sie mit, und sie standen vor ihrem Fenster und trugen jedes Jahr die schönsten Rosen, weiß und roth.
sentences.l: But the two little rose-trees she took along with her, and they stood before her window and bore every year the loveliest roses, white and red.
sentences.i: But the two little rose-trees she took with her, and they stood before her window and bore the loveliest roses every year, white and red.
sentences.n: “mitnehmen” — to take along (separable). “roth” = 1857 spelling of rot, closing the tale on the two sisters’ colours.

glossary.messing: das Messing — brass (the metal; plain High German, not a dialect word)
glossary.volk: das Volk — folk, people (here scornful, ‘rabble, lot’; plain High German, not Low German)
